title: Evolving the cloud-native foundation for the next generation of AI
summary: Discover how Azure is advancing cloud-native infrastructure to help organizations build, run, and optimize applications and agents at scale.
body_markdown:
## Building a cloud-native foundation for AI


The relationship between model innovation and AI infrastructure has never been more clear; as AI becomes more capable, the platform underneath it matters even more. Agents are fundamentally changing how applications work, and with that, what organizations need from the cloud.


[Learn how to build a cloud-native AI foundation](https://developer.microsoft.com/en-us/reactor/series/S-1692/)


[Cloud-native practices gave organizations the scale, flexibility and resilience](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/solutions/cloud-native-apps/) to build a generation of distributed applications. Agents build on that foundation, but they work differently, placing new demands on it. Unlike applications designed around more predictable workflows,[agents behave in entirely new ways, gathering information and deep intelligence from across the business](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/solutions/ai/) , using tools, making decisions, and coordinating work across long-running processes. To complete complex tasks, they pause for approval, respond to new information in real time and change course as conditions evolve. All this changes what the platform needs to deliver.


Customers need infrastructure that adapts as demand changes, applications that remain reliable as work becomes more dynamic, and the visibility and control to understand what is happening across the system. Meeting those needs doesn’t mean starting over, but it does require that the cloud-native foundation organizations already rely on, to evolve.[Compute, storage and networking need to work together](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cloud-computing/finops/framework/optimize/architecting) . Application platforms need to make it easier to build and run AI workloads. Open technologies need to give customers flexibility without adding unnecessary complexity.


The platform decisions organizations make today are increasingly strategic, shaping how effectively they can put AI to work for their business. Evolving the cloud-native foundation is essential to helping organizations get more from AI today while giving them the flexibility to take advantage of new capabilities as they emerge.


## Optimize infrastructure for AI workloads


The true measure of AI infrastructure is the useful work it enables. AI workloads rarely place the same demands on infrastructure from beginning to end.[Different parts of the work may need accelerated compute, CPUs, fast access to data or connectivity](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/solutions/high-performance-computing/ai-infrastructure) across applications and environments. The answer isn’t simply more capacity, but rather, to[match the right resources to the right work at the right time](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cloud-adoption-framework/ai/infrastructure/compute) .


That makes coordination across the infrastructure extremely important. Compute, storage and networking need to work together as demands change. When they do, teams can spend less time managing infrastructure and more time focused on the applications and outcomes that matter to their business.


Economics matter, too. Infrastructure needs to be tuned to the demands of the application and the business value it delivers,[with the right balance of performance, reliability and cost](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/blog/cloud-cost-optimization-how-to-maximize-roi-from-ai-manage-costs-and-unlock-real-business-value/) across the complete workload.


[Basecamp Research](https://www.microsoft.com/en/customers/story/26652-basecamp-research-ltd-azure-container-registry) is one example. The company used Azure to assemble 9.7 trillion nucleotides for EDEN, its therapeutic-design models, and reported laboratory validation across three therapeutic applications within about three weeks. In this example, AI didn’t simply require more infrastructure, it needed AI infrastructure that was coordinated and designed around the outcome – bringing together the compute, data and platform capabilities needed to move complex work forward.


As Glen Gowers, co-founder of Basecamp Research put it: “To really be successful here, we need those three ingredients to come together. We need someone scaling the data; that’s us. But someone who really knows how to scale models and scale compute is Microsoft.”


Leadership takeaway: Measure success by the useful work AI completes. Judge infrastructure investment by the performance, reliability and cost of delivering those outcomes, with compute, storage and networking operating as one system.


## Turn open-source innovation into production capability


Open technologies have long helped drive cloud innovation, and AI is accelerating that pace. New models, frameworks and cloud-native technologies give organizations more choice in how they build and adapt applications.


That opportunity builds on an established cloud-native foundation. Gartner forecasts that by 2028, 95% of new AI agent deployment will use Kubernetes.1 Reusing established components can shorten the path to production, allowing developers to focus on differentiated business capabilities rather than rebuilding the foundation.


More choice can also bring more complexity. Taking advantage of open-source innovation often requires specialized expertise to integrate, manage and maintain technologies in production. That expertise is hard to find and even harder to scale. We need to make these capabilities accessible to more businesses, without requiring every organization to build and maintain that expertise themselves.


Azure helps reduce that burden. Services like[Azure Kubernetes Service](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/aks/what-is-aks) give teams access to open-source innovation while helping manage the complexity and risk of running it in production. This makes it easier for more businesses to take advantage of open technologies while preserving the flexibility to adapt with changing needs.


Leadership takeaway: Choose a platform that helps turn open-source freedom into business advantage.[Preserve the ability to adapt and optimize while reducing the expertise and operating effort](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/blog/azure-iaas-how-to-design-build-and-optimize-cloud-infrastructure-for-long-term-cost-optimization-efficiency/) required to sustain those choices in production.


## Align AI infrastructure costs with business value


As more organizations put AI into production, understanding the economics becomes increasingly important. AI investment starts with an expectation of business value: faster decisions, more responsive services or greater capacity to get useful work done. Then, it’s evaluating whether the value justifies the investment to deliver it.[FinOps](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cloud-computing/finops/overview) can help teams understand that return and make more informed decisions in this area.


For customers, that starts with understanding the full investment required to run AI applications and how to optimize it as workloads scale. Models represent a significant expense, with token usage and agent behavior influencing spending. Compute, storage, networking and operations also factor into the equation. Considering these together helps customers make more informed decisions about where to optimize.


[Learn FinOps best practices for compute](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cloud-computing/finops/best-practices/compute)


Teams can’t simply place their bets on spending less. They need to carefully consider that a more capable model or additional infrastructure that costs more may be the right choice if it produces greater value long-term. Teams need to understand the full cost, establish ownership and put guardrails in place as they scale. From there, they can use business outcomes to decide where to optimize and where to invest.


Leadership takeaway: Manage AI investment against the business return it needs to deliver. Evaluate model and platform costs together, then use evidence of outcome value to decide where to optimize and where to invest.


## Transform cloud operations with agentic AI


Operations teams are already stretched thin, keeping critical services running while balancing competing priorities and constant change. AI adds new complexity, and it also creates an opportunity to change how those environments are managed.


Cloud-native operations gave teams a new model for managing infrastructure, bringing increased automation, visibility and resilience.[Agentic operations build on that foundation](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/sre-agent/) , bringing deeper intelligence across applications and infrastructure by connecting signals from otherwise disconnected systems. This helps teams identify issues earlier and resolve them faster, while increasing automation and continuously improving how their environments perform; all within the tools they already use.


Over time, AI can help operations teams move from reacting to problems toward anticipating and addressing them before they disrupt the business. As these capabilities mature, more actions can be automated within defined controls, with people remaining in the loop and accountable for critical decisions. When operations teams have greater reach without additional manual effort, reliability, performance and cost are continuously improved while critical services remain uninterrupted.


Leadership takeaway: Invest in operations that can anticipate problems and coordinate action across the environment. Expand autonomy as capabilities are validated, with clear controls and human accountability protecting critical business services.


[Automate operations with Azure SRE Agent](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/sre-agent/)


## Build a cloud-native AI foundation on Azure


Azure serves as the foundation customers need to put AI to work at scale. That means infrastructure designed around the complete workload, access to open innovation without unnecessary complexity, and a clear view of cost and business value. Greater intelligence across cloud operations helps teams anticipate issues and continuously improve how their environments perform as application needs evolve.


[We’re continuing to invest in capabilities across Azure](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-gb/solutions/ai/?ef_id=_k_CjwKCAjwirLWBhBBEiwAlItbEiofqa5DDqkdgm6LDQnspxBsKug9QALCXOsCCeA2BYKp1Q2v8naV_RoCfewQAvD_BwE_k_&OCID=AIDcmmo7vzpajg_SEM__k_CjwKCAjwirLWBhBBEiwAlItbEiofqa5DDqkdgm6LDQnspxBsKug9QALCXOsCCeA2BYKp1Q2v8naV_RoCfewQAvD_BwE_k_&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=23504081703&gbraid=0AAAAADcJh_uggBwd2EZDje1Ybccm3N8Nl&gclid=CjwKCAjwirLWBhBBEiwAlItbEiofqa5DDqkdgm6LDQnspxBsKug9QALCXOsCCeA2BYKp1Q2v8naV_RoCfewQAvD_BwE) that give customers greater flexibility in how they build and run AI applications. From[secure, isolated environments for agents](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/container-apps/sandboxes-get-started) to simpler application deployment and the ability to run workloads across cloud and edge environments, these investments help customers take advantage of new capabilities without adding unnecessary operational complexity.


[Get started with Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS)](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/products/kubernetes-service/)


AI is changing what applications can do, and Azure has already evolved to support that shift. The cloud platform has to evolve with them. Years of focused engineering investment have built the foundation for some of the most advanced AI workloads running today, with continued innovation to support what comes next.


## Build for the next generation of AI


Platform value compounds when improvements reinforce one another: faster information access keeps compute productive, operational insight exposes waste, and open technologies preserve room to adapt. The leadership task is to make those gains work together. That is the next chapter of cloud native: a foundation that turns advances in AI into dependable business value.
